chapter: Learning drums and Roy Eldridge's band
title: George Hornsby turns to church music
summary: Hornsby, a fine pianist and writer of songs Fletcher Henderson played, became religious and played only church music.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: So I gigged around with George Hornsby for quite awhile, and then something strange happened to George. He became religious and he joined the church and began to play just church music.
Was he a white boy?
No, he was a colored boy. After He'd written so many beautiful things.
Songs, even?
Yes, he just turned right around and went religious, and he started playing in the churches. So then I left George --
Did he ever end up doing anything?
Not really. He just stayed in the church all the time. He never came out.
Did he become a preacher?
No, just a musician in -- he wanted to be close to the church.
Fancy that.
Can you imagine?
It's unusual.
And A wonderful pianist.
Fancy that.
And he had written many good songs that Fletcher Henderson played.
Which ones, do you remember?
Oh. I think Hawk took one of his tunes.
Oh, not, 'Hello, Lola,' or, 'One Hour.'
No, it was something like, 'Changes,' or
something, it was called.
Oh. And made it with the band?
Yeah, just went through the keys.
Not, 'Queer Notions.' Because 'Queer Notions' went through a heck of a lot of changes.
That could have been it, because --
Oh, did he write a number like that?
Very modern chords.
Yes. That was around -- that was about '32.
Fancy that. That'd be the right time.
